messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Navy Officer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 33

He is 34, a Navy officer, married, and used to thinking of himself as someone who stays composed when other people lose theirs. Before the storm, that is how he understands his role at work and at home. He likes routine, clear chains of command, and the comfort of believing that preparation matters. He and his wife live near the coast because of his assignment, and in the weeks before the disaster he follows the forecasts with the practiced attention of someone trained to respect weather without dramatizing it. He helps secure the house, fills containers with water, checks batteries, and reassures his wife that they are ready.

When the hurricane makes landfall, it becomes clear very quickly that “ready” is a relative word. The wind sounds, in his memory, less like weather than like something alive pushing against the walls. At first he moves through the house with purpose, checking windows, bringing in towels, making calls while the power still flickers on and off. Then the water begins coming in faster than he expects. The street disappears. A neighbor shouts from outside, and somewhere nearby glass breaks. He remembers the smell most vividly now: wet drywall, sewage, gasoline, and the briny odor of floodwater moving where it should not be.

He gets his wife into the attic space when the lower floor starts filling. He tells himself what he tells junior officers in emergencies: focus on the next task, not the whole picture. But in the attic, with the dark pressing in and the house creaking beneath them, he feels something he still has trouble naming. It is not only fear. It is the sickening realization that his rank, his training, and his confidence do not matter against water rising inch by inch. He uses a tool to break through part of the roof in case they need to climb out. His hands shake so badly that he cuts himself without noticing until his wife points out the blood. They wait for hours listening to distant voices, sirens, and the thud of helicopter blades that seem both near and unreachable. He keeps scanning, calculating, listening for structural collapse. Even after they are rescued by boat, he cannot shake the image of their house half-submerged, as if the ground itself has betrayed them.

In the months afterward, he returns to duty sooner than his wife thinks he should. He tells her he needs to get back to normal, though “normal” turns out to be something he can no longer find. At work he performs well enough to avoid attention. He is early, uniform pressed, paperwork complete. But he notices he is changed in small, embarrassing ways. During heavy rain he loses track of conversations and feels his chest tighten before he is even aware of the sound on the roof. If an alarm goes off unexpectedly, his whole body reacts before his mind catches up. He starts checking exits in every building and feeling irritated when others seem oblivious.

Sleep becomes its own battle. He dreads nights when the wind picks up because his body seems to remember before he does. He wakes abruptly, already sitting up, heart pounding, sometimes convinced for a second that water is rising around the bed. His wife reaches for him and he pulls away before he realizes where he is. Afterward he feels ashamed, then distant. She wants to talk about that night and about the losses that followed—the damaged house, the months of displacement, the way neither of them felt settled afterward—but he keeps conversations practical. Insurance. Repairs. Logistics. He tells himself he is protecting her from his own reactions, though she experiences it as him disappearing while sitting right beside her.

He avoids the waterfront now unless duty requires it. He used to find the ocean calming; now he studies it like a threat. On days off, instead of going out with friends, he stays busy with drills of his own making: checking emergency kits, reorganizing supplies, watching forecasts repeatedly. He knows it is excessive, and that knowledge does not help. His wife teases him gently at first, then stops when she sees he is not really joking back. She says he is always “on,” and he knows she is right. In restaurants he chooses the seat facing the door. In traffic during storms, he grips the wheel so hard his forearms ache.

What troubles him most is not just the fear but the change in how he sees himself. He has built a life around competence and steadiness. Now he finds himself snapping at subordinates over minor mistakes, then feeling guilty because the anger is out of proportion. He feels detached during moments that should be easy—dinner with his wife, a phone call with his parents, a quiet Sunday morning. He goes through the motions while part of him remains elsewhere, in that dark attic listening to the house strain around him.

He does not describe himself as broken. He says instead that he has “never fully stood down” since the storm. Even in calm weather, some part of him is still waiting for the water to rise.
